articles.title: Amanda Redman: ‘My most embarrassing moment? Getting caught doing a pretend Bafta thank you speech’
articles.summary: The actor on a terrible accident as a toddler, her bossy nature, and feeling too old to play a Shakespearean heroine. Born in Brighton, Amanda Redman, 69, studied at Bristol Old Vic theatre school. She starred in the TV comedy drama El C.I.D.
body: When were you happiest? I am happiest when I have my daughter and granddaughter with me.

What is your earliest memory? Being in hospital. I was standing up in a cot and we were being asked what we wanted for lunch. I think it was Great Ormond Street. I had managed to pull a cauldron of boiling turkey and vegetable soup all over me when I was 18 months old, and I spent five years of my life in various hospitals.
Which living person do you most admire and why? Barack Obama, for his decency. I felt real hope when he was elected, which has been dashed now.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? Meanness of spirit.

articles.title: ‘Anchors Aweigh’ Review: A Cynical Comedian Reflects on His Youth in an Abridged Mockumentary
articles.summary: In Matt Barats’ “Anchors Aweigh,” a caustic alt-comedian is left adrift after his failed proposal, prompting him to revisit old footage from his college days and ruminate on his arrested development.
body: Matt Barats brings mordant wit to both sides of the camera, for better or worse.

When the acerbic lead rents a boat on a Marina by a New York airport, the movie gestures toward a mockumentary in the vein of John Wilson, or a send-up of Ross McElwee, but its secondary and tertiary characters — marina residents whom Barats interacts with — seldom stick around long enough to make a lasting impact. It isn’t long before the story snaps back towards malformed romance, the self-conscious tone of which does little more than exacerbate its narrative flaws.

articles.title: ‘Trees Are Watching’ Review: Eva Green Fights A.I. Generated Horrors in Self-Serious Misfire Boarded by Martin Scorsese
articles.summary: Bahman Ghobadi directs some fascinating performances in “Trees Are Watching,” his horror movie based on the Kurdish legend of people being reborn as trees and living second lives as furniture.
body: Iranian new wave mainstay Bahman Ghobadi tries his hand (and his prompts) at a midnight movie.

The film begins with a flashback to three young Kurdish girls in Mardin, Turkey discussing the aforementioned superstition, before one of them, Darya (Green), returns years later from abroad with her Deaf, nonverbal daughter Connie (Neva Kuş) to perform anthropological research in the area. Kuş is a firecracker of a performer, adding lively dimensions to the chilling atmosphere when things go bump in the night, and Connie begins hearing strange, unsettling sounds through her hearing aid.

A pair of tall trees sway outside the home Darya has rented, a modern expansion of where her childhood friends Nihal and Spin used to live. Inside, Darya’s dog acts aggressively toward an ornately carved chair, which Connie soon claims has been moving on its own. Before long, the chair becomes a specter of sorts, seemingly possessed by a spirit from Darya’s past, which unravels in vivid flashbacks that don’t entirely seem motivated — they’re Nihal and Spin’s memories for the most part, not Darya’s — but which detail an intriguing backstory nonetheless.
points: Bahman Ghobadi directs some fascinating performances in “Trees Are Watching,” his horror movie based on the Kurdish legend of people being reborn as trees and living second lives as furniture.

articles.title: White House Blocks CNN and MS NOW Journalists From Entry and Confiscates Their Badges After Donald Trump Bans Networks
articles.summary: President Donald Trump doesn’t like the coverage of him by CNN, MS NOW and Politico — and as of Saturday, the White House started enforcing the president’s ban on those news organizations from accessing the facility.
body: CNN and MS NOW said their staffers were denied access to the White House Saturday morning.

CNN said in a statement: “Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.”

MS NOW also said some of its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds Saturday morning. The network, formerly known as MSNBC, said it will “take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”
In a report on the network, MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Garnder described what happened when she arrived to try to get in to the White House.

articles.title: ‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?
articles.summary: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement.
body: This Sunday, the curtain falls on the Toronto film festival, the last of the three big autumn showcases – alongside Venice and Telluride – that are launchpads for award campaigns. And as the dust settles on the red carpets, one name rises above the others as destined for sure-fire glory: Andrew Scott.

The Irish actor, 50 next month, is now not only considered a lock for a leading actor Oscar nomination but almost certain to take the prize next spring. Should he win, he will become the first out gay actor to do so in the Academy’s almost 100-year history.

If that’s a fact that seems astonishing today, it would have felt an inevitability in 1989, when the film for which Scott has been so praised is set. In Elsinore, he plays Ian Charleson, the dashing Scottish star of films including Chariots of Fire and Gandhi. Charleson had been given his first role three years before Chariots by Derek Jarman, but excised it from his CV (leading to a lifelong rift, depicted in Elsinore). Muting his sexuality was then considered essential in the pursuit of stardom. Yet despite such curation – and his undeniable talents – Charleson never reached the level of fame he felt he deserved.

articles.title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary
articles.summary: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign. First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as…
body: The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.

articles.title: Spain’s SETT Drives $521 Million Investment Push to Build Global Audiovisual Players
articles.summary: No Spanish industry initiative is likely to drive more conversation at this year’s San Sebastián Festival than the latest moves by the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT).
body: In other ways, SETT, which is part of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation, also harbors a revolution. Since the 1940s, Spanish governments have offered subsidy grants and loans for individual films, and from around 2015, tax breaks on shoots in Spain.

In contrast, SETT invests up to 10 years in companies with a portfolio of productions, requiring co-investment from private-sector partners, and looking to give them an edge in the international market. It also backs private-sector investment vehicles.
“We are moving from an era of encouraging an ecosystem to consolidating a truly international audiovisual industry,” says González Veracruz.

Eleven of 15 SETT investments have been made public to date, with beneficiaries including animation sector leaders ( Anima Kitchent, Amuse Animation, Planeta Junior), new Spain-based production companies ( Good Films Studios Spain, Ítaca Films Madrid, Moonlighting Studios Spain), post-production facilities ( Lazona Audiovisual Hub, the Refinery) and a full chain-of-value production-distribution player (Impulse Studio).

articles.title: John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’
articles.summary: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete. As mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has frequently demonstrated impressive media savvy, but arguably nothing has proved his genius for in-the-know promo more…
body: It was because of that scaffolding episode, released in October 2020, that I, like some smart Mamdani staffers, began to perceive the sidewalk shed shadowing my block not as an inevitable fixed entity but an obtrusive, if well-intentioned, symptom of neglect. Shortly after the mayor’s video, said scaffolding miraculously came down – revealing, to my shock, a three square-wide swath of concrete that had not seen the sun in six years.

When I credit Wilson for this upgrade, in person at a film office in Manhattan, he reacts with a modest “I’ll take it,” as dry as the dusty footprints of the recently departed metal poles. Fitting, for though that newly revealed concrete, speckled with old gum and anonymous residue, is certainly better, if not exactly beautiful, perhaps only Wilson could see it as cinematic. His debut feature film, The History of Concrete, takes on the granddaddy of all urban materials, tugging wry insights on our terminal human condition out of the crumbling facades of New York’s most pervasive substance.

articles.title: ‘American Hostage’ Review: Jon Hamm and Giovanni Ribisi in an MGM+ Kidnapping Thriller With Lots of Potential but Little Payoff
articles.summary: Shawn Ryan and Eileen Myers ('The Night Agent') adapt the podcast focusing on a 1977 kidnapping in Indianapolis and the trusted radio host caught in the middle.
body: MGM+ ‘s American Hostage is a TV show based on a podcast about the power of radio, a chaotic media-hopping smorgasbord that feels oddly appropriate when you watch the eight-part series that flirts with a number of contemporary topics but ends up being mostly well-acted, over-extended nostalgia for landline telephones and manageable institutional corruption.

The series is set in 1977, and if you’ve seen Gus Van Sant’s 2025 Dead Man’s Wire, you already know a somewhat fictionalized version of the story, which was the subject of the first season of the American Hostage podcast from Criminal Content.

Hamm plays Fred Heckman, an Indianapolis news radio legend. Heckman, who has a wonderfully supportive marriage to Barbara ( Mireille Enos ) plus three kids who are irrelevant to the series, is described on bus ads as “the most trusted voice in news.”

Heckman has largely given up on the reporting that launched his career and, after 22 years in Indianapolis, he’s weighing a lucrative offer to move to CBS Radio in New York City. Then he becomes part of the biggest story to hit Indianapolis in years.
points: Shawn Ryan and Eileen Myers ('The Night Agent') adapt the podcast focusing on a 1977 kidnapping in Indianapolis and the trusted radio host caught in the middle.

articles.title: When Hollywood’s Major Studios Threatened to Leave California — For Florida
articles.summary: A Democratic Socialist was running for California governor and the studio chiefs balked and said they'd pack up their moving trucks and leave. They were bluffing in 1934. Now...
body: Southern California seems to have been terraformed by the Creator to attract the motion picture industry: the mild, sunny weather conducive to outdoor shooting; the boundless variety of natural scenery (ocean, mountains, desert, farmlands) that can double for any location on earth; the diverse population of ready-made extras, and, at least in the first decades, the open shop policies of the city fathers (no pesky trade unions).

Little wonder that the pioneers of the medium ditched the cold, clammy, and crowded precincts of New York and New Jersey to light out for the picture-perfect vista. Soon enough, modern factories staffed by a pool of extraordinarily talented artists sprang up to manufacture quality-controlled product. Why would any filmmaker want to leave such prime real estate and glamorous expertise?

articles.title: Resident Evil Director Zach Cregger Has A Stealthy Cameo That You Probably Missed
articles.summary: If you're looking for director Zach Cregger's cameo in his new Resident Evil movie, you won't see it. But if you keep your ears open, you'll hear it.
body: Zach Cregger has asserted himself as a modern horror master in just a handful of short years. "Barbarian" put him on the map, but "Weapons" took him to another level when that film became a huge, mainstream, Oscar-winning hit. He's come a long way since co-directing the comedy flop "Miss March." His latest movie, a reboot of the "Resident Evil" franchise, has proved that he can work well within a pre-existing universe, and Cregger decided to include himself in that universe via a sneaky cameo.

The movie follows Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier who unwittingly finds himself in an action-packed, non-stop race for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in chaos. Taking place mostly in Raccoon City, it fits into the timeline of the video games alongside "Resident Evil 2." It's not directly adapting any of the games, instead opting to tell a brand new story inside that universe.
